newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower, led again by gold.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower, led again by gold.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower across the board Wedneday, led again by gold which slid to new four-year lows.

"The consensus is universally bearish in gold, and with producer hedging apparent, against a backdrop of seasonally slow demand during the summer, any upward correction will likely meet overhead selling," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
COMEX August gold ended down $2.80 at $332.20 an ounce, after seeing a further life-of-contract low at $332.10 near the close.
But COMEX gold estimated final volume was a relatively light 28,000 lots, as the market begins to wind down ahead of the U.S. Independence Day holiday Friday, traders said.
COMEX will close early Thurday and will be closed Friday for the July 4 U.S. holiday.

COMEX gold open interest has continued to expand on the downtrend though this week, edging up a further 1,767 lots Tuesday to 196,108 contracts, after seeing its highest levels since February on Monday as funds have increased short positions.

"We're not seeing any real bargain hunting yet, and with light producer hedging going on, the funds probably don't feel under any pressure to cover short positions ahead of the holiday weekend," one bullion banker said.
"Inevitably it looks like gold is going to $326.00 (basis spot) eventually," he said.

Technically, the downtrend in COMEX August gold has accelerated this week, with a standard 14-day ADX indicator edging up to 30 pct, and 20-day historical volatility up to 9.6 percent from 6.0 percent mid-June.

But oscillators closed at oversold levels, suggesting a bounce may be near short-term, analysts said. A standard nine-day relative strength indicator (RSI) ended at 20 percent, while a five-day slow stochastic was now also well below 20 percent.

In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $331.10/60, after seeing a London afternoon fix at $332.15. Earlier gold had fixed at $331.45 at the morning fix, the lowest since March 24, 1993. In New York Tuesday, spot gold had ended around $333.70/20.

Both short-term and longer-term implied lease rates for gold rose further Wednesday, reflecting both hedge fund short selling in the OTC market and producer hedging, with the two-to-six month maturities the most active, bankers said.
One month implied lease rates for gold rose to 1.78 pct Wednesday and one year rates were up to 2.01 pct.
COMEX September silver ended down 3.3 cents at $4.640 an ounce, after a burst of selling at the close, but held above the contract lows seen Monday at $4.630.
In the bullion market, spot silver ended quoted around $4.63 an ounce, with support seen around $4.60, a level which has held for most of 1997.
In platinum group metals (PGMs), NYMEX October platinum lost $5.20 at $406.70, while NYMEX September palladium lost down $1.80 at $174.50.

"PGMs shouldn't go down too much more, since we haven't seen any Russian metal deliveries yet, and when deliveries do begin, pent up demand will likely keep prices firm, or at least there's probably still more upside potential than downside risk," Smith Barney's Rinehimer said.
"Russia is not viewed as reliable supplier anymore, their own stockpiles are in decline, and the PGM market is heading into a supply/demand deficit situation," he said.
Earlier Wednesday, Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, reiterated it would resume shipments of PGMs around July 10, under the recently-signed term-contract with Japanese trade houses.
Meanwhile, the physical PGM market remained tight, with one month platinum lease rates still around 60 pct and one month palladium rates were around 90 pct.
Russia supplies about 60 pct of the world's palladium and 20 pct of its platinum, and exports have been suspended since December 1996, pushing spot prices and forward rates sharply higher this year.
